newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Sheep ship fire unlikely to damage trade - AMLC.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Sheep ship fire unlikely to damage trade - AMLC.

text.p: Growing controversy in Australia over 67,000 live sheep on a vessel which caught fire bound for Jordan is unlikely to have longer-term repercussions on Australia's A$500 million live sheep and cattle export trade, according to the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC).
The fate of the sheep is expected to be known soon with a rescue vessel now on its way to the Panama-flagged Uniceb, AMLC spokesman Chris Rowley said.
Australia's live animal export trade has come under heavy criticism from animal welfare groups and unionists since the vessel caught fire.

The International Transport Workers' Federation issued a statement on Thursday calling on the AMLC and Minister for Primary Industries John Anderson to ban livestock exports on flag of convenience (FOC) ships after the death of a seafarer on the Uniceb.
Rowley said the rescue ship should be arriving late this afternoon Australian eastern time. Until it did, it would not be known if the sheep were alive or dead, he said.
"It's an extremely unfortunate accident. We've got a good safety record and hopefully long-term we'll be able to continue to show that," he said.
"We're as concerned as anyone, particularly with the animal welfare considerations.
"But the trade's been going for a long while and every effort has been made to make it as safe as possible," Rowley said. "Some accidents just can't be foreseen.
"We certainly will be looking at trying to figure out what caused this and if it can be averted in the future," he said.
It was believed that the incident would not have a longer-term impact on the trade, he said.
Australia's live sheep trade began in the 1950s with small shipments of sheep to Southeast Asia. Shipments to the major market of the Middle East began in the 1960s.
In 1995/96 Australian live sheep exports reached 5.47 million head, worth more than A$207 million.

The Middle East accounts for 99 percent of Australia's shipments of live sheep. Jordan is the largest importer, taking more than 1.57 million head in 1995/96, up 30.7 percent and worth an estimated A$58.2 million.
In 1995/96 the total volume of Australia's live sheep shipments fell by 8.2 percent while value increased by 11 percent.
The trend continued in July with export volumes well below the 600,000 head exported in the same month of the previous year, AMLC said in a statement.
Mortality rates were low, averaging 1.8 percent per voyage, it said.
The 14,990 tonne Uniceb, which caught fire on Monday bound for the Jordanian port of Aqaba from Fremantle, Western Australia, is owned by Lugano-based Sistrin Services.
One crew member was killed and 54 rescued as a result of the fire, according to Lloyds shipping service.

"Animal Liberation and the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals have called for a ban on live sheep exports, we are calling for a ban on FOC shipping," International Transport Workers' Federation/Australia coordinator Trevor Charles said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
